title: Shrinking the sample space
objectives: Compute a conditional probability by counting what is left
Explain why the condition shrinks the denominator

screens.title: Shrinking the sample space
screens.prose: You roll two dice and learn something about the result. Some outcomes become impossible, so every chance has to be measured again on what is left.
Two fair dice give 36 outcomes, all equally likely. Each cell is one outcome: the row is the first die, the column is the second.
screens.question: Shade every outcome where the total is 8.

hints.text: If the first die shows 3, what must the second die show?
Totals of 8 sit on one diagonal, and it starts in row 2.
Go row by row. A first die of 2 needs a 6, and a 3 needs a 5. Carry on up to 6. Row 1 cannot reach 8.

feedback.correct: Five of the 36 outcomes add to 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try every first die from 1 to 6, and check that each shaded pair adds to 8.

byKey.missed-double: You missed (4, 4). A double is one outcome, and it counts.
byKey.r1c6: (1, 6) adds to 7, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r2c5: (2, 5) adds to 7, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r3c4: (3, 4) adds to 7, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r3c6: (3, 6) adds to 9, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r4c3: (4, 3) adds to 7, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r4c5: (4, 5) adds to 9, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r5c2: (5, 2) adds to 7, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r5c4: (5, 4) adds to 9, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r6c1: (6, 1) adds to 7, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.
byKey.r6c3: (6, 3) adds to 9, not 8. Check each shaded pair again.

explain.text: You shaded the five cells from (2, 6) down to (6, 2). A first die of 1 cannot reach 8, so row 1 stays empty. That makes $P(\text{total is } 8) = \tfrac{5}{36}$.

screens.prose: New roll. A friend peeks and tells you the first die shows 5. The marked cells are the totals of 8 from the last screen.

enter.caption: 6 outcomes left: the first die is 5

screens.question: What is the chance the total is 8 now?

options.why: That is the chance before the news. Only the 6 cells in row 5 are still possible.
That divides by all 36 outcomes. Only the 6 cells in row 5 are still possible.
That is the chance the total is not 8. Count the cells that do reach 8.

hints.text: Which cells are still possible once you know the first die is 5?
Only row 5 is still lit. How many cells does it have, and how many are marked?
Row 5 has 6 cells. One of them, (5, 3), adds to 8. Divide the marked cells by 6.

feedback.correct: One of the 6 cells left, (5, 3), adds to 8.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only inside row 5, the cells still possible.

explain.text: You counted inside row 5, the only row left once the first die is 5. One of its 6 cells, (5, 3), adds to 8. So the news moved the chance from $\tfrac{5}{36}$ to $\tfrac{1}{6}$.

screens.prose: Another roll. This time your friend only says: at least one die shows a 5.

enter.caption: At least one die shows a 5

screens.question: How many outcomes are left?

widget.label: Number of outcomes left
widget.accept: 11 exactly. Row 5 and column 5 share one cell: $6 + 6 - 1 = 11$.

hints.text: How many cells are in row 5? How many are in column 5?
One cell sits in both row 5 and column 5.
Row 5 has 6 cells and column 5 has 6. The corner (5, 5) is in both, so count it once.

feedback.correct: Row 5 plus column 5, with the corner counted once.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells that are still lit, each one once.

byKey.corner-twice: You counted the (5, 5) cell twice. Look at the corner.
byKey.corner-removed: Row 5 and column 5 share only one cell, (5, 5). Take it away once, not twice.
byKey.one-row: That is one row. The 5 can also be on the second die.
byKey.everything: That is every outcome. Rolls with no 5 are ruled out.
byKey.no-five: That counts the outcomes with no 5. You want the ones that are left.

explain.text: You counted row 5 and column 5, and the corner (5, 5) belongs to both. Counting it once gives $6 + 6 - 1 = 11$. The news shrank the sample space from 36 outcomes to 11.

screens.prose: Same news as before: at least one die shows a 5. Now look for a total of 10.
screens.question: What is the chance the total is 10?

options.why: That treats one die as fixed at 5. You only know at least one is a 5, so 11 cells are possible.
You divided by 12, so the corner (5, 5) was counted twice. The cross has 11 cells.
That counts every way to make 10 among all 36 outcomes. Two of them have no 5, so they are gone.

hints.text: Which pairs add to 10? Which of them contain a 5?
Only one cell in the cross adds to 10.
The pairs adding to 10 are (4, 6), (5, 5) and (6, 4). Only (5, 5) is in the cross, and the cross has 11 cells.

feedback.correct: Only (5, 5) adds to 10, out of 11 cells.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cells in the cross that add to 10, out of the 11 cells in the cross.

byKey.fixed-die: That treats one die as fixed at 5. You only know at least one is a 5, so 11 cells are possible.

explain.text: Your $\tfrac{1}{11}$ counts one cell, (5, 5), out of the 11 in the cross. The other ways to make 10, (4, 6) and (6, 4), contain no 5, so they dropped out. Before the news the chance was $\tfrac{3}{36} = \tfrac{1}{12}$.

screens.prose: You counted the outcomes where both things happen, out of the outcomes still possible. That is a conditional probability: $P(A \mid B)$, the probability of $A$ given $B$. Now turn your counts into probabilities.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $= \dfrac{|A \cap B| / 36}{|B| / 36}$, divide top and bottom by 36
$= \dfrac{P(A \cap B)}{P(B)}$, each count over 36 is a probability

hints.text: Which line is exactly what you did with the cells?
The middle line has to turn each count into a probability.
Start from the counts. Divide both $|A \cap B|$ and $|B|$ by the same number, 36. Then name each fraction as a probability.

feedback.correct: The same factor top and bottom keeps the value.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from what you counted, then change both counts the same way.

byKey.divide: Dividing by 36 only makes sense once you have the counts. Start from the line you counted.
byKey.probs: The probabilities come from dividing the counts by 36, so that line comes last.

explain.text: You divided both counts by 36, which leaves the fraction unchanged. With your numbers, $A$ is a total of 10 and $B$ is at least one 5: $P(A \mid B) = \tfrac{1/36}{11/36} = \tfrac{1}{11}$. The last line needs no counting, so it also works when outcomes are not equally likely.

screens.prose: Time for an experiment. You will roll two dice many times and keep only the rolls with at least one 5. Predict first, then roll.

state.caption: Filter: keep a roll when at least one die shows a 5

screens.question: Of 1,000 rolls, about how many survive the filter?

widget.label: Rolls that survive, out of 1,000
widget.accept: any whole number from 280 to 330. Expected: $1000 \times \tfrac{11}{36} \approx 305.6$

hints.text: What fraction of the 36 outcomes has at least one 5?
The filter keeps the same outcomes as the cross you counted earlier.
11 of the 36 outcomes survive, so expect about $1000 \times \tfrac{11}{36}$ rolls.

feedback.correct: About 11 in every 36 rolls contain a 5. Now roll to test it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A roll survives when it lands in the cross: 11 of the 36 outcomes.

byKey.ten-share: That uses $\tfrac{1}{11}$, the share of kept rolls with total 10. You want the share of all rolls that are kept.
byKey.one-die: That is the chance one particular die shows 5. Either die can show it.
byKey.corner-twice: That counts the (5, 5) roll twice: 12 in 36. The cross has 11 cells.
byKey.everything: Rolls with no 5 are thrown away, so fewer survive.

explain.text: 11 of the 36 outcomes contain a 5, so about $\tfrac{11}{36}$ of rolls survive: $1000 \times \tfrac{11}{36} \approx 305.6$. Roll 1,000 to see how close the experiment comes.

screens.prose: Two stocks, A and B, each finish the day up or down with equal chance, independently. After the close you hear one fact: at least one of them finished up.
screens.question: What is the chance both finished up?

options.why: That is the chance before the news. Both down is now ruled out.
That assumes you know which stock rose. You only know at least one did, so three outcomes remain.
That is the chance exactly one stock rose. Both up is one of the three outcomes left.

hints.text: Which of the four outcomes does the news rule out?
One of the four outcomes is impossible once you know at least one stock rose.
Three outcomes remain, each equally likely. Count the ones where both are up.

feedback.correct: Both up is one of three equal outcomes left.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rule out the outcome the news makes impossible, then count.

explain.text: You ruled out both down, which leaves three equal outcomes: both up, only A up, and only B up. Only one has both up, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{3}$, not $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

ideas: News rules outcomes out. The outcomes still possible form the new sample space.
With equally likely outcomes, count inside what is left: $$P(A \mid B) = \frac{|A \cap B|}{|B|}$$
Divide top and bottom by the total, and the rule works for any outcomes, equally likely or not.

formula.name: Conditional probability
formula.note: Defined only when $P(B) > 0$: you cannot condition on something impossible.

summary.trap: “At least one is a 5” is not “the first is a 5”. The first leaves 6 outcomes; the second leaves 11.

quiz.prose: Two fair dice are rolled. You are told the total is 7.
quiz.question: What is the chance that one of the dice shows a 3?

options.why: That counts only (3, 4). The 3 can be on either die, so (4, 3) counts too.
That is the chance of a total of 7 given a 3 is showing. The condition runs the other way here.
That divides by all 36 outcomes. A total of 7 leaves only 6.

feedback.correct: (3, 4) and (4, 3), out of 6 ways to make 7.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the six ways to make 7 first.

explain.text: A total of 7 leaves six outcomes, from (1, 6) to (6, 1). Two of them, (3, 4) and (4, 3), contain a 3. So the chance is $\tfrac{2}{6} = \tfrac{1}{3}$.

quiz.prose: A fair six-sided die is rolled. You learn the result is even.
quiz.question: What is the chance it is greater than 3? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance, as a fraction or decimal
widget.accept: any form equal to $\tfrac{2}{3}$, or a decimal that rounds to 0.67.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only 2, 4 and 6 are left. Count the ones above 3.

byKey.before: That is the chance before you learned it was even. Only 2, 4 and 6 are left.
byKey.one-face: Of 2, 4 and 6, two are greater than 3, not one.

explain.text: Learning the result is even leaves 2, 4 and 6. Two of those, 4 and 6, are greater than 3. So the chance is $\tfrac{2}{3}$.

quiz.prose: Stocks A and B each finish up or down with equal chance, independently. This time you learn that A finished up.
quiz.question: What is the chance both finished up?

options.why: That answers “at least one rose”. Here you know A rose, so only B is uncertain.
That is the chance before any news. Knowing A rose leaves two outcomes.
That is the chance at least one stock rises. You already know A did.

feedback.correct: Knowing A rose leaves two equal outcomes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fix A as up, then look at B.

explain.text: Knowing A rose leaves two equal outcomes: both up, and only A up. B rose in one of them, so the chance is $\tfrac{1}{2}$. Compare the lesson: “at least one rose” left three outcomes and gave $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
